render.title: NADH and FADH2 as electron donors
render.body:
Both NADH and FADH2 are electron carriers produced earlier in cellular respiration. They deliver electrons to specific entry points in the electron transport chain embedded in the inner mitochondrial membrane.

NADH drops off its electrons at Complex I (NADH dehydrogenase). This is the first and largest complex in the chain. When NADH is oxidised back to NAD+, the energy released drives the pumping of four protons from the matrix into the intermembrane space.

FADH2 donates its electrons at Complex II (succinate dehydrogenase). This complex does not pump protons directly, so FADH2 contributes less to the proton gradient than NADH does.

From Complex I and Complex II, electrons pass to a mobile carrier called ubiquinone (coenzyme Q), which carries them to Complex III. From there, another mobile carrier called cytochrome c shuttles them to Complex IV, where they finally reduce oxygen to water.

Because NADH enters at Complex I and FADH2 enters at Complex II, each NADH ultimately drives more proton pumping and therefore produces more ATP than each FADH2.
summary_bullets: NADH donates electrons at Complex I, triggering the pumping of four protons per NADH.
FADH2 donates electrons at Complex II, which does not pump protons, so FADH2 yields less ATP than NADH.
Electrons then flow through ubiquinone, Complex III, cytochrome c, and Complex IV before reducing oxygen to water.
